subject: People in each job in NYC
footnote_text: No agency publishes a yearly series of NYC workers by job (the state's wage table keeps only its latest year), so we estimate it: NYC payroll jobs in each industry (New York State Department of Labor), split into jobs using the state's mix of jobs in that industry (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics). Where NYC's mix differs from the state's, our count is off; registered nurses and home health aides are examples. It counts payroll jobs, so the self-employed are left out, and the years between 2019 and 2025 cover slightly fewer jobs where a code is missing that year. Pages also show the published count for the New York metro area, which has about twice NYC's workers. On Getting in, jobs added count only jobs with an NYC number in both 2019 and 2025.
short_text: NYC people in each job are our estimate, from payroll jobs by industry and the state's mix of jobs.

subject: Openings a year marked “our estimate”
footnote_text: New York State's 2022–2032 forecast has no usable number for 24 degree-level jobs (18 of the 164 we rank, and 6 “All other” groups), but it does give a total for each job group; 38 more named jobs have no NYC forecast at all. We divided each group's leftover total among its jobs, by how many people do each job in the New York metro area and how fast each job grows and turns over nationally (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics).
short_text: The state gave only a total for this job's group, so we split it.

subject: Openings a year
footnote_text: Openings a year are a forecast by the New York State Department of Labor: the average number of jobs to fill each year from 2022 to 2032, counting new jobs plus jobs left open when people retire or change careers (the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics method). Someone moving to another employer in the same kind of job is not counted, so actual hiring is higher. For a shrinking job, openings are lower than the number of people leaving, because the jobs lost are subtracted.
short_text: Openings a year: a forecast of new jobs plus jobs left when people retire or change careers.

subject: Self-employed workers
footnote_text: Payroll job counts leave out self-employed people, so jobs with many freelancers (writers, designers, consultants, performers) are undercounted.

subject: Transportation and warehousing, 2024
footnote_text: In 2024, transportation and warehousing gained about 43,000 payroll jobs, and 128,000 “new hires” in the first quarter, because of a change in how employers were recorded (the state's monthly survey shows the sector flat), not because they hired. Its 2024 hiring rates can't be compared with 2019's; the 2019 rates are shown beside them, and job pages use the 2019 rate.

subject: Health care hiring, 2025
footnote_text: In the second quarter of 2025, health care and social assistance shows about 261,000 “new hires” and 277,000 people leaving while its jobs stayed flat, in every borough. On April 1, 2025, New York moved its home-care program for self-directed aides (CDPAP) from about 600 agencies to one statewide employer and re-registered more than 195,000 personal assistants; the quarter records that transfer, not hiring. The sector's 2025 hiring rates can't be compared with earlier years.

subject: Hiring and people leaving
footnote_text: Hiring and leaving counts come from the U.S. Census Bureau (Quarterly Workforce Indicators). They cover private employers with unemployment insurance, all ages, with the five boroughs added together, and the Census Bureau adds a little random noise to protect privacy. They describe industries, not jobs: a job's “turnover” is the turnover of the industries it works in, not of the job itself.

subject: Openings a year
footnote_text: Openings a year come from the New York State Department of Labor's 2022–2032 projection for NYC, built from 2022 data: before the 2023–2026 slowdown in job postings, and before the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics cut its outlook for more than 40 jobs partly because of AI (2025–35 projections, Table 1.12). For 24 job groups the state's file had no usable number, so about 13% of these openings are our split of its group totals (marked “our estimate”). On 2026-10-02, Indeed's index of job postings (February 2020 = 100) stood at 85 for the New York metro area and 104 for the United States. The state has not yet released a 2024–2034 projection for NYC.
short_text: Projected from 2022 data, before job postings slowed (NY-area postings on 2 Oct 2026: 15% below Feb 2020).

subject: Entry wage
footnote_text: The entry wage is the New York State Department of Labor's figure for the average pay of the lowest-paid third of all workers in a job in NYC. The state surveys employers through May 2025 and states the wages in early-2026 dollars. It is not what new graduates are offered. The NYC median pay is not a job offer either. The Overview shows the entry wage of the middle degree-level job, so half of the jobs start higher.
short_text: Entry wage: the average pay of a job's lowest-paid third of workers, not a new graduate's offer.

subject: Living wage
footnote_text: The living wage is the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Living Wage Calculator's line for one adult with no children in the New York metro area, 2026: $65,510 a year before taxes ($31.50 an hour). Like the state's wages (early-2026 dollars), it is for 2026 and before taxes. New York City's own True Cost of Living measure for a single adult is $70,334 a year (2022 data, taxes and savings included). About 1 in 4 openings in degree-level jobs, and about 4 in 5 in associate's-entry jobs, are in jobs whose entry wage is below MIT's line. It is a yardstick for one adult, not a judgment of any job.
short_text: Living wage: what one adult needs for basic costs in the NY metro area, before tax (MIT, 2026).

subject: Experience asked
footnote_text: Experience asked is the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' national rating of the work experience in a related job that employers typically consider necessary to start (its education and training categories). It is not any one employer's hiring rule.
short_text: Experience asked: the related work experience BLS rates as typically needed to start; not a hiring rule.

subject: Pay over time
footnote_text: Pay over time is the published pay series for the New York metro area (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics), in 2025 dollars using the New York-area consumer price index. For a group of jobs, the change shown is the average of each job's own median (or lower-quarter) change, weighted by its 2025 NY-metro workers; it is not the change in one group median. BLS cautions against reading its pay survey as a time series (it redrew the metro area in 2024 and changed methods), so small changes are within the noise.

subject: Does a job take beginners?
footnote_text: No public source says whether an opening is for a beginner or someone experienced. We show three signals side by side and never combine them: the experience the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics says is typical, the share of NYC residents working in the job who are aged 22 to 29 (U.S. Census Bureau survey, 2020–2024), and the share of O*NET respondents who say a new hire needs a month or less of related experience. They often disagree.

subject: Skills and knowledge
footnote_text: Skill and knowledge ratings come from O*NET, the U.S. Department of Labor's job database: national ratings (knowledge by workers and experts in the job, skills by O*NET's trained analysts), applied here to NYC jobs.

subject: Census estimates
footnote_text: What graduates do comes from the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey: estimates for NYC residents, each with a 90% margin of error. Groups with fewer than 30 survey answers are too small to show; they are marked, never dropped. The field is the bachelor's field; a graduate degree may be in another field.

subject: Graduate-degree pay gap
footnote_text: “People with a graduate degree earn X% more” describes a gap, not a payoff: it doesn't account for who chooses graduate school, which field they study, tuition, or years out of work.

subject: Majors with no single job path
footnote_text: Some majors' graduates hold the jobs the program-to-job list links them to less than 1.5 times as often as all NYC graduates do (U.S. Census Bureau survey; psychology, political science, criminal justice, general business), so no one job is their path. For them we show no graduates-per-opening number; their page lists the jobs the program-to-job list links them to, which are only part of where their graduates work.
short_text: “Graduates work across many jobs”: no one job is the path; the jobs listed are only part of where they work.

subject: Graduates per opening
footnote_text: Graduates per opening compares first majors awarded by all NYC colleges (CUNY highlighted) with projected NYC openings. Each major's graduates are spread over the jobs it leads to by those jobs' openings (spreading them equally is shown as a range). NYC employers hire from everywhere, and NYC graduates also leave the city.

subject: More competition
footnote_text: “More competition” means more NYC graduates than projected openings in the jobs a major leads to. It is not a judgment of the major. The growth axis is the projected change for 2022–2032; the actual change for 2019–2025 is shown beside it.

subject: 2024 degree counts
footnote_text: 2024 degree counts (degrees awarded July 2023–June 2024, first majors) are early figures from the U.S. Department of Education's college data and may still change. Associate's degrees fell sharply from 2019 to 2024, mostly in majors with no linked job at their level, led by liberal arts, which students often take before a bachelor's. Some changes since 2019 are colleges moving programs between major codes. Degree years run July to June, so 2019 is July 2018 – June 2019. All NYC colleges are the 107 colleges in the five boroughs that reported associate's or bachelor's degrees to the Department of Education for 2024: the 19 CUNY colleges that award them, private colleges like NYU and Columbia, and three SUNY colleges. A college can report a similar program under another major code.
short_text: Years run July–June (2024 = July 2023–June 2024), first majors; “all NYC colleges” includes CUNY; early counts.

subject: AI exposure
footnote_text: AI exposure is a research estimate, not government data: the share of a job's tasks that people have been seen doing with one AI assistant (Anthropic Economic Index, March 2026). Exposure is not job loss. A major's exposure is the weighted average over the jobs it leads to (or, for majors whose graduates mostly work elsewhere, over where its graduates actually work); the share in High-exposure jobs is shown because those jobs often split into very high and very low.

subject: AI exposure
footnote_text: AI exposure on the job page is the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' relative AI exposure rating (2025–35 projections, published 2026-08-27): Low, Moderate, High or Very high, set by clustering five research measures, including Anthropic's. BLS says it is relative to other jobs and not a forecast of job growth or decline. “AI use seen” is the second layer: the time-weighted share of the job's tasks seen in work use of one AI assistant (Claude; assisted use counts half) (Anthropic Economic Index, March 2026), a research estimate. Neither is job loss.
short_text: AI exposure: BLS's relative rating (2026). AI use seen: Anthropic research (not government).

subject: AI exposure
footnote_text: AI exposure is the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' relative AI exposure rating for every job in its 2025–35 projections (published 2026-08-27): four groups, Low, Moderate, High and Very high, made by clustering five research measures (Felten–Raj–Seamans, Eloundou and others, Eisfeldt and others, Anthropic, Microsoft). BLS says the rating is relative to other jobs and is not a forecast of job growth or decline. The shares weight each job by its NYC openings a year (projection, 2022–2032).
short_text: AI exposure: BLS's relative rating (2026), from five research measures; not a forecast of jobs.

subject: Job postings
footnote_text: Postings are a private estimate of online job ads in New York State by job group (Revelio Labs), not government data. In August 2025 the company re-sorted ads between groups, so one-year changes start in August 2025 and say “since the August 2025 data break”. The 22 job groups show a pattern, not a cause.

subject: Similar jobs with lower AI exposure
footnote_text: “Similar jobs with less AI use seen today” are lower on Anthropic's research measure of AI use (BLS's rating may be the same); they use similar knowledge and skills and pay at least 90% as much. They are ranked by how alike their O*NET knowledge and skill profiles are (68 elements). “Close” means a correlation of 0.82 or more (the top 5% of all pairs of jobs); “possible” means 0.75 to 0.82. Being similar doesn't mean people move between them: no NYC data on job moves exists. Pay is the NYC median; there is no upper limit, so similar jobs that pay more are kept, with the difference shown.

subject: What “leads to” means
footnote_text: A major “leads to” a job when the U.S. Department of Education's program-to-job list (the NCES CIP–SOC crosswalk) says the program prepares people for that job, kept where the job usually starts with that degree or at least 15% of its workers nationally stop at that degree (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics). A job group the list links only in part (one of its detailed jobs) counts by that part's share. It says what a program prepares for, not where its graduates were hired, and other majors lead to the same jobs.
short_text: “Leads to”: the government's program-to-job list says the major prepares for the job; it isn't hiring data.

subject: Five kinds of major
footnote_text: Each major is one of five kinds, by how the program-to-job list links it. Leads to degree-level jobs: most openings in its linked jobs are in this study's 225 occupations (a job group linked only in part counts by that part's share). Leads mostly to jobs outside the study: most are in jobs that usually start with less schooling or with a graduate degree. Graduates work across many jobs: its graduates hold its linked jobs less than 1.5 times as often as all NYC graduates do, so no one job is its path. No job at its level: the list links it only to jobs that don't usually start with its degree and where under 15% of workers stop at that degree. It is named by where those jobs sit: Linked jobs need more schooling (every one usually starts with more than its degree), Linked jobs need less schooling (every one starts with less), or No linked job at this level (some of each). Liberal arts associate's degrees, which students often take before a bachelor's, are the largest group; we have no data on who transfers or goes on to graduate school. No job link: the list doesn't link it to any job.
short_text: Kind: where most openings in a major's linked jobs fall, in or outside the study, or why it has no job path.

subject: Openings in a major's jobs
footnote_text: Openings a year belong to the jobs, not to the major. Other majors lead to the same jobs, so the openings a major's jobs have are shared, and adding them up across majors would count the same openings more than once.
short_text: Openings belong to the jobs, which other majors also lead to: they are shared, not this major's alone.

subject: “1 yr+ training”
footnote_text: In the “Experience asked” column, “1 yr+ training” marks a job where the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics says new workers need no related work experience but usually need more than 12 months of on-the-job training (9 of the 225 jobs, such as Actuaries and Financial Examiners); “internship” marks a job that usually takes an internship or residency (4, such as Architects).
short_text: “1 yr+ training”: no experience asked, but BLS says new workers train on the job over a year (or in an internship).
